name: NAET allergy elimination

card.summary: An acupressure-and-muscle-testing system, devised in 1983, that practitioners use to address allergy-related complaints, including skin reactions that affect how the skin looks.
card.note: Major allergy bodies advise against its diagnostic method; it is not a substitute for allergy testing.

quick.overview:
NAET (Nambudripad's Allergy Elimination Techniques) is an alternative-medicine practice that combines muscle testing with acupressure or acupuncture. People who use it usually seek relief from allergy-type symptoms, and some hope that calmer reactions will mean clearer, less irritated skin.

Its founder describes allergies as energy blockages, and practitioners treat one suspected substance at a time. Allergy organisations that have reviewed it report that its muscle-testing method has not been shown to identify allergies, and no clinical trials supporting it have been published.
quick.how: A session typically involves a practitioner testing muscle strength while the client holds a vial containing a suspected allergen, followed by acupressure or acupuncture along meridian points. Clients are then asked to avoid that substance for a set period and may return for retesting.
quick.risks: Allergy bodies including the AAAAI and the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy have advised against it; the latter called it potentially dangerous. Reviewers warn that people with severe food allergies who test themselves after sessions could risk anaphylaxis, and that unwarranted dietary restriction could lead to nutritional shortfalls.

lead: NAET (Nambudripad's Allergy Elimination Techniques) is an alternative-medicine system that its practitioners use to address allergies and related complaints. For people with a skin focus, such as reactive or irritated skin, the appeal is that calmer reactions to everyday substances might mean a clearer, less inflamed complexion. [1]

It was devised in 1983 by Devi Nambudripad, a California-licensed chiropractor and acupuncturist, who said she developed the idea after a reaction to carrots eased following a self-administered acupuncture treatment. [1]

Reviews by allergy specialists have examined applied kinesiology, NAET's main diagnostic tool, and report that it has not been shown to diagnose allergies; several professional bodies advise against the method. [1]

chain: Muscle testing selects a suspected allergen
Acupressure is applied while holding it
Practitioners say reactions to it fade
angle.text: Proponents describe NAET as retraining the body's response to substances such as foods, which they say would reduce allergy symptoms, including skin reactions. Its appearance link is therefore indirect and rests on the practitioners' claims.

infobox: Not endorsed by major allergy organisations

paras: Practitioners use what they call neuromuscular sensitivity testing to pick out suspected allergens. The client holds a glass vial containing the substance during acupressure or acupuncture, rests for about 20 minutes still holding it, and is retested. Clients are advised to avoid the substance for at least 25 hours and may return for retesting between 25 hours and seven days later. [1]

NAET holds that allergies are energy disturbances, or blockages of qi along meridians, caused by what it calls repulsive electromagnetic fields between a person and a substance. It counts allergens as including emotions and colours. Nambudripad has suggested that 95 percent of human ailments arise from some sort of allergy. [1]

Reviews by Niggemann and Gruber (2004), Wüthrich (2005) and Teuber and Porch-Curren (2003) concluded that applied kinesiology is not effective for diagnosing allergies, and Teuber and Porch-Curren wrote that no studies support these techniques. Bodies that advise against it include the European Academy of Allergology and Clinical Immunology (1999), NICE, the American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology (2008) and NIAID (2010). [1]

The Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (2007) called it a potentially dangerous technique. Reviewers have cautioned that people with severe food allergies who test themselves after NAET could face anaphylaxis, and critics such as Stephen Barrett argue that dietary restrictions based on non-existent allergies could cause nutrient deficiencies and, in children, social problems and eating disorders. [1]
No studies found. Published reviews of applied kinesiology, the diagnostic method NAET relies on, are described above. [1]
